pool.builds_on: The paper’s demonstration that compositional modifications can tune the microstructure and properties; here, the concept is extended by using a reactive element (Y) to target oxidation resistance while preserving key strength elements.
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis proposes a bulk alloying modification that strategically substitutes a less critical element (Nb) with a reactive element (Y) to form a self-healing, oxide‐adhesion–promoting interfacial layer, which was not attempted in the original study.

fields.hypothesis: Bulk Minor Yttrium Substitution on the Nb Sub-Lattice to Enhance Oxide Adhesion Without Compromising Strength
fields.material_initial_state: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr cast HEA with a BCC structure that exhibits acceptable ductility and high‐temperature strength but poor oxygen resistance.
fields.intervention: Substitute about 2–3 atomic % of Nb with yttrium (Y) so that the overall composition shifts slightly to HfNb(1–x)YxTaTiZr (x ≈ 0.02–0.03) while keeping Ta and Hf levels intact.
fields.conditions: Prepare the modified alloy by casting and homogenization under the same conditions as the baseline. Expose specimens to full air at 1000 °C for 100 hours, and perform tensile tests at room temperature and at 1000 °C with strain rates between 10⁻⁴ and 10⁻² s⁻¹.
fields.structural_mediator: The formation of a submicron-scale Y-enriched interfacial region at the oxide–substrate boundary that promotes formation of a coherent, adherent, and slow-growing protective oxide scale.
fields.mechanism: Yttrium is a well-known reactive element that segregates to oxide interfaces when added in small amounts. In this HEA, by substituting a small fraction of Nb (which is less critical for yield strength than Ta), Y can migrate to the oxide/alloy boundary during high-temperature exposure, lowering oxide growth stress and delaying spallation. Consequently, this controlled reaction limits oxygen ingress and maintains oxidation resistance without sacrificing the mechanical properties controlled by Ta and Hf levels.
fields.predicted_outcome: A reduction in oxidation weight gain and oxide scale thickness by roughly 30–50% compared to the unmodified equiatomic alloy, while the room-temperature ductility and high-temperature yield strength remain within ±15% of the baseline.
fields.baseline: Untreated cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr HEA that develops rapid, nonprotective oxidation in air at 1000 °C.
fields.boundary: The Y addition must be kept low (around 2–3 at.%) and substituted from Nb to prevent perturbing the primary strength contributors (Ta and Hf) and to maintain the BCC phase stability.
fields.uncertainty: While the reactive element effect of Y is established in other high-temperature alloys, the precise segregation behavior and interfacial chemistry in this multicomponent HEA require experimental confirmation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of cast specimens: one set with the standard equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy and a second set with 2–3 at.% Y substitution for Nb. Subject both sets to air exposure at 1000 °C for 100 hours. Characterize the oxide scale (thickness, morphology, adherence via SEM/EDS and XRD) and perform tensile tests at room temperature and 1000 °C.
measurements: Oxidation weight gain
Oxide scale thickness and adhesion
Tensile yield strength and ductility
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Y‐modified alloy does not achieve at least a 30% improvement in oxidation metrics (lower weight gain/scale thickness) or exhibits mechanical properties that deviate by more than ±15% from those of the baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C8
pool.builds_on: The high thermal stability of the refractory BCC phase demonstrated in the paper indicates that the base alloy can endure a diffusion treatment without loss of bulk performance. This hypothesis adapts established pack aluminizing techniques from superalloy processing to the HfNbTaTiZr system.
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis proposes applying a pack aluminizing treatment—a well-established method in superalloy processing—to generate an in situ, diffusion-induced surface aluminide that converts into a protective Al2O3 scale, providing an innovative single-intervention approach to overcome the oxygen resistance limitation of the alloy.

fields.hypothesis: Pack Aluminizing to Form a Surface Aluminide Layer with Subsequent Al2O3 Scale Formation: A pack aluminizing treatment applied to cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will promote the diffusion of Al into the surface, forming an intermetallic aluminide layer. Upon exposure to high-temperature oxidizing conditions, this surface layer will transform into a protective Al2O3 scale, greatly enhancing oxygen resistance while preserving the alloy's bulk mechanical properties.
fields.material_initial_state: Cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr having good ductility and high-temperature yield strength but prone to rapid oxidation in air.
fields.intervention: Subject the as-cast alloy to a pack aluminizing process using an Al-rich powder mixture (with suitable activators) at elevated temperature.
fields.conditions: Pack aluminizing at approximately 900 °C for 4 hours in a mildly reducing pack environment; subsequent oxidation exposure at 1000 °C in air for 100 hours; mechanical testing performed at room temperature and at 1000 °C under strain rates of 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹.
fields.structural_mediator: A diffusion-induced surface aluminide layer that converts upon oxidation into a stable, adherent Al2O3 scale.
fields.mechanism: During pack aluminizing, Al diffuses into the surface of the alloy forming an aluminide intermetallic layer. When the treated alloy is subsequently exposed to high-temperature air, the aluminide layer preferentially oxidizes to produce a compact and adherent Al2O3 layer. This scale acts as a diffusion barrier to oxygen, significantly reducing further oxidation of the base alloy.
fields.predicted_outcome: A dramatic reduction in oxidation—evidenced by a thinner oxide scale and lower weight gain (targeting around a 50% reduction relative to the untreated sample)—while maintaining key mechanical properties (with variations within ~5–10% of the untreated alloy).
fields.baseline: The untreated cast alloy develops a thick, porous oxide scale under high-temperature air exposure that degrades mechanical performance.
fields.boundary: Effective for high-temperature oxidation conditions at ∼1000 °C and mechanical loadings characterized by strain rates between 10⁻⁴ and 10⁻² s⁻¹.
fields.uncertainty: The success of pack aluminizing is sensitive to process parameters (temperature, time, pack composition) and overdiffusion or formation of brittle phases must be avoided; the long-term cyclic oxidation resistance remains to be verified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HfNbTaTiZr samples: one group undergoes pack aluminizing and one group remains untreated. Expose both groups to 100 hours at 1000 °C in air. Characterize the surface layer via SEM/EDS and XPS to confirm the formation of an aluminide layer and subsequent Al2O3 scale; measure oxidation weight gain and perform mechanical tests (tensile and compressive) at both room temperature and 1000 °C.
measurements: Surface phase composition and morphology (SEM/EDS, XPS)
Oxide scale thickness and uniformity
Weight gain during oxidation (TG analysis)
Mechanical properties (yield strength, ductility from tensile/compressive tests)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pack aluminized samples do not show a distinct aluminide layer that transforms into a protective Al2O3 scale, or if they do not exhibit a significant reduction in oxidation or show mechanical property degradation exceeding ~10% compared to untreated samples, the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C9
pool.builds_on: The approach builds on the concept of tailoring interstitial and substitutional elements to optimize phase stability and strengthening (as in PMC5227964), extending it to surface-engineered oxidation protection.
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces a controlled surface modification (aluminizing) to overcome oxygen degradation of HfNbTaTiZr, a strategy not explored in the paper, while aiming to preserve the alloy’s favorable mechanical properties.

fields.hypothesis: A surface aluminizing treatment via pack cementation will form a dense, adherent alumina (Al₂O₃) scale on cast HfNbTaTiZr, significantly slowing oxygen ingress at high temperatures while preserving the alloy’s intrinsic mechanical performance.
fields.material_initial_state: Cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibiting 8–16% room-temperature ductility and high-temperature yield strength (163–530 MPa at 1000 °C).
fields.intervention: Apply a surface aluminizing treatment by pack cementation. This involves exposing the cast alloy to an aluminum-rich powder mixture at an elevated temperature (e.g., 900–950 °C) for a controlled short duration to enrich only the surface with aluminum.
fields.conditions: Treatment temperature ~900–950 °C for a duration of 2–4 hours in an inert or slightly reducing atmosphere; subsequent exposure tests at 1000 °C in an oxygen-containing atmosphere (e.g., air) for periods on the order of tens to hundreds of hours; mechanical tensile tests at room temperature and 1000 °C under strain rates of 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹.
fields.structural_mediator: A thin, continuous alumina (Al₂O₃) layer formed on the surface.
fields.mechanism: The introduced Al diffuses and reacts with oxygen at the surface to form a slow-growing, dense Al₂O₃ scale that acts as a barrier to oxygen diffusion. This protective layer retards further oxidation without altering the bulk microstructure responsible for the excellent ductility and high-temperature strength.
fields.predicted_outcome: A substantial improvement in oxygen resistance (i.e., reduced oxide scale growth and slower oxygen penetration) at high temperatures, while maintaining comparable room-temperature ductility and high-temperature yield strength relative to the untreated alloy. The scale is expected to reduce oxidation by at least an order of magnitude in the given exposure time compared to untreated samples.
fields.baseline: Untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr shows poor oxygen resistance due to rapid internal oxygen uptake, compromising high-temperature performance.
fields.boundary: The treatment must be optimized to limit bulk Al uptake; over-treatment or excessive Al diffusion might alter phase stability. The protective effect may diminish if thermal cycling causes scale spallation.
fields.uncertainty: While the principles of alumina scale protection are well documented in other refractory alloys (e.g., Ni aluminides as in TXT::wikipedia::Nickel_aluminide::005), the quantitative improvement in HfNbTaTiZr needs to be experimentally verified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr specimens—one with the surface aluminizing treatment and one untreated. Expose both sets to an oxygen-containing atmosphere (air) at 1000 °C for 100 hours.
measurements: Measure oxide scale thickness and composition via SEM/EDS and XRD.
Perform tensile tests at room temperature and 1000 °C to assess ductility and yield strength.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aluminized specimens do not show a significantly thinner and more uniform Al₂O₃ scale and if their high-temperature mechanical properties deteriorate relative to untreated samples, the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C10
pool.builds_on: The mechanism identified in PMC8911703 that slower oxidation (as seen in the HT3 condition) leads to superior oxide scales is applied here to a cast, coarse-grained HfNbTaTiZr by promoting selective Hf oxidation.
pool.what_is_new: It introduces a low oxygen pre-oxidation step specifically tailored for a cast HfNbTaTiZr alloy, targeting the formation of a Hf-rich barrier oxide, differing from approaches developed for nanocrystalline sputtered films.

fields.hypothesis: Pre-oxidize the cast HfNbTaTiZr alloy under low oxygen partial pressure at moderate temperature to form a thin, continuous HfO2‐rich barrier that retards further oxidation.
fields.material_initial_state: Cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr with a coarse-grained as-cast microstructure exhibiting rapid oxidation and spallation at high temperatures.
fields.intervention: Expose the alloy to a controlled atmosphere with a very low O2 content (e.g., an Ar:O2 ratio of 95:5) at 500 °C for 1 hour to selectively oxidize Hf at the surface, forming a thin, adherent HfO2-rich nanolaminate oxide.
fields.conditions: Pre-oxidation: 500 °C for 1 hour in Ar:O2 (95:5). Followed by final oxidation exposure at 1000 °C for 4 hours in air. Mechanical testing conducted at room temperature (8–16% tensile ductility) and at high temperature (yield strength of 163–530 MPa at strain rates of 10^−4–10^−2 s^−1).
fields.structural_mediator: A dense, ultrathin HfO2-rich oxide scale that forms a coherent barrier, minimizing the high-diffusivity paths (e.g., grain boundaries) normally prevalent in a coarse cast microstructure.
fields.mechanism: At a moderated temperature with diluted oxygen, the slower cation diffusion preferentially oxidizes Hf due to its high oxygen affinity, forming a stable and adherent HfO2 layer. This pre-formed barrier, by reducing further oxygen ingress and cation movement during subsequent high-temperature exposure, prevents oxide scale spallation. This builds on the paper’s finding that slowing oxidation kinetics improves the quality of the oxide scale by reducing defects (PMC8911703, especially Sections 3.2–3.3).
fields.predicted_outcome: A significant reduction in oxide scale spallation and oxygen uptake during a 1000 °C, 4-hour exposure, with retention of the alloy’s useful mechanical properties relative to untreated cast samples.
fields.baseline: Untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr which rapidly develops poorly adherent, spalled oxide scales when exposed to high temperatures in oxidizing atmospheres.
fields.boundary: The approach must be effective for exposures at 1000 °C for 4 hours in air and not induce mechanical property degradation (maintaining tensile ductility of 8–16% and the expected yield strength range).
fields.uncertainty: The optimal oxygen partial pressure, treatment duration, and temperature for a cast coarse-grained alloy are not fully established, and the diffusion kinetics of Hf in this system require further quantification.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of cast HfNbTaTiZr samples. One set receives the pre-oxidation treatment (500 °C, 1 hour in Ar:O2 95:5) and the other set is left untreated. Both sets are then exposed to oxidation at 1000 °C for 4 hours in air. Following this, evaluate the oxide scale morphology using SEM/TEM, perform XRD/XPS for phase analysis, measure weight gain via thermogravimetric analysis, and conduct tensile tests at room and high temperature.
measurements: SEM/TEM imaging of the oxide scale
XRD and XPS to confirm HfO2 phase and scale adhesion
Thermogravimetric (weight gain) measurements
Tensile tests (yield strength and ductility)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-oxidized samples do not demonstrate a significantly thinner, more coherent, and less spalled oxide scale (with correspondingly lower oxygen uptake) while still maintaining the baseline mechanical properties compared to untreated samples, the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C11
pool.builds_on: The concept of leveraging minor reactive element additions to improve oxide scale adhesion observed in other high-temperature alloys, extended to the multi-principal element system as discussed in PMC9506522.
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis proposes a subtle compositional modification by introducing yttrium—a reactive element not previously used in HfNbTaTiZr—to form a more protective oxide scale, thereby overcoming oxygen resistance limitations without affecting the established mechanical performance.

fields.hypothesis: Add a minor reactive element, yttrium (Y), into the equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy to improve oxygen resistance via the reactive element effect while minimally perturbing the alloy’s intrinsic high-temperature mechanical properties.
fields.material_initial_state: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr as-cast state with acceptable room-temperature ductility (8–16%) and high-temperature yield strength (163–530 MPa at 1000 °C).
fields.intervention: Modify the alloy composition by adding a small amount (~1 at%) of Y (with a corresponding slight reduction in one of the other element percentages to maintain near-equiatomic ratios).
fields.conditions: Casting and homogenization as per the baseline procedure, with subsequent conventional thermomechanical processing to preserve the microstructure; test under service conditions at 1000 °C in an oxygen-containing atmosphere, at strain rates of 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹.
fields.structural_mediator: An improved surface oxide scale that incorporates Y at the oxide grain boundaries.
fields.mechanism: Yttrium is known to segregate at oxide scale boundaries, enhancing the adhesion and integrity of the native oxide (likely HfO₂/TiO₂-based) formed during oxidation. This reactive element effect reduces the rate of oxygen diffusion into the bulk, thereby improving high-temperature oxidation resistance without compromising the combined mechanical performance established by the equiatomic matrix.
fields.predicted_outcome: An improved oxygen resistance with a lower oxidation rate (observable as reduced weight gain in oxidation tests) while maintaining room-temperature tensile ductility (8–16%) and high-temperature yield strength within the ±10% range of the untreated alloy.
fields.baseline: The untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits poor oxygen resistance during high-temperature exposure despite its favorable mechanical performance.
fields.boundary: The benefit is expected provided the Y content is kept low (~1 at%) to avoid formation of brittle intermetallics or significant microstructural changes; higher Y additions may lead to embrittlement.
fields.uncertainty: While the beneficial effect of reactive elements in oxidation resistance is well documented in other systems, the quantitative impact of 1 at% Y on the specific oxide scale formation and its long-term stability in HfNbTaTiZr is uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Cast two alloy variants: one equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr and one with ~1 at% Y addition. Subject both to prolonged oxidation tests at 1000 °C in an atmosphere with standard oxygen content under controlled tensile loading conditions.
measurements: Oxidation kinetics (weight gain measurements).
Surface and cross-sectional microstructural analysis using TEM/SEM to evaluate oxide scale adherence and thickness.
High-temperature tensile test comparison for yield strength and ductility.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Y-containing alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in oxidation resistance (i.e., similar or higher weight gain) or its mechanical performance deteriorates relative to the baseline (beyond a 10% margin), the hypothesis is rejected.

top3.label: C6
top3.builds_on: The finding that high-temperature annealing strongly influences atomic-scale ordering is extended here by modifying only the surface composition to foster the growth of a protective oxide, thereby directly addressing oxygen ingress.
top3.what_is_new: Instead of altering the bulk nanostructure via high-temperature annealing, this hypothesis introduces a single-step pack-cementation surface treatment that selectively enriches the surface with Al, enabling the formation of a protective alumina scale during service.

fields.hypothesis: Pack-Cementation Surface Aluminization to Form a Protective Alumina Scale
fields.material_initial_state: Cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr with its as‐cast microstructure exhibiting 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility and yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C.
fields.intervention: Expose the alloy to a pack-cementation treatment in which the sample is embedded in an Al-rich powder mixture (with suitable activators like NH4Cl) and heated at an optimized temperature, e.g., ~900 °C for 2–4 hours in an inert or slightly reducing atmosphere.
fields.conditions: Treatment performed under controlled atmosphere (e.g., flowing N2) at ~900 °C for 2–4 hours, ensuring the diffusion of Al only into a thin surface region (~5–10 μm). Subsequent high-temperature service exposure in air at 1000 °C for up to 100 hours with mechanical loading at strain rates of 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹.
fields.structural_mediator: An Al-enriched surface layer that, upon exposure to oxygen, forms a thin, continuous, and adherent alumina (Al₂O₃) scale.
fields.mechanism: The pack-cementation treatment diffuses a small amount of aluminum into the alloy’s surface. During later high-temperature exposure in air, the slightly enriched surface preferentially oxidizes to form a protective Al₂O₃ layer. Alumina is known for its excellent oxygen diffusion barrier properties and high stability (TXT::wikipedia::Superalloy::002). The treatment is confined to the surface so that the bulk dislocation-driven strengthening and ductility remain unaffected, thus overcoming the poor oxygen resistance without sacrificing mechanical performance. This approach builds on the understanding of oxide scale formation while leveraging surface chemical modification.
fields.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated cast samples, treated samples should exhibit a significant reduction in weight gain due to oxidation (on the order of a 40–50% reduction) and display a dense, adherent alumina scale upon microscopic examination, all while retaining the original mechanical performance.
fields.baseline: Untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr which shows rapid oxidation in air, leading to degradation of surface integrity and limited high-temperature applicability.
fields.boundary: The treatment parameters must be controlled so that the aluminized depth remains superficial (≈5–10 μm) to avoid altering the bulk microstructure. Excessive aluminum diffusion or overlong treatments may form thick scales or intermetallic phases which could degrade mechanical properties.
fields.uncertainty: The exact degree of oxidation protection (in percentage reduction of weight gain) and the optimal process window (time and temperature) require experimental calibration; however, the protective nature of alumina in superalloys provides moderate prior evidence.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two cohorts of samples: one set undergoing the pack-cementation aluminization treatment and one untreated. Expose both groups to high-temperature air (1000 °C) for 100 hours under controlled mechanical loading (strain rates of 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹). Characterize the oxide scale via SEM/TEM/XPS for continuity and composition, measure weight gain per unit area, and perform mechanical tests before and after exposure.
measurements: Oxide scale thickness, continuity, and composition (via SEM, TEM and XPS).
Weight gain per unit surface area to assess oxidation kinetics.
Mechanical properties (yield strength and tensile ductility) before and after high-temperature exposure.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated samples do not achieve at least a 40% reduction in oxidation weight gain and/or if their mechanical properties (ductility and yield strength) deviate significantly (beyond the reported range) from the untreated baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.

top3.label: C5
top3.builds_on: The need highlighted in PMC7514121 for further composition modification to mitigate high-temperature oxidation, combined with the known beneficial effects of reactive element additions (e.g., Y) in high-temperature alloys.
top3.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces a minor yttrium addition—a compositional modification not explored in the paper—to induce in-situ surface passivation via Y2O3 formation, specifically tuned to the unique BCC high-entropy alloy microstructure.

fields.hypothesis: Introduce a minor yttrium addition (~1–2 at%) to the cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy to promote the in‐situ formation of a protective Y2O3 scale during high‐temperature exposure.
fields.material_initial_state: As‐cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr with a homogeneous dendritic BCC microstructure and documented room-temperature ductility (8–16%) and high-temperature yield strength (163–530 MPa at 1000 °C).
fields.intervention: Modify the starting composition by adding 1–2 at% yttrium, keeping the remaining elements equiatomic, and process via standard vacuum-arc melting.
fields.conditions: Expose the modified alloy to air at 1000 °C for 50 hours, then perform room-temperature tensile tests (strain rate ~10⁻³ s⁻¹) and high-temperature compression tests under the same strain rate range (10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹).
fields.structural_mediator: A thin, self-forming Y2O3 scale on the surface that preferentially forms due to yttrium segregation and its strong affinity for oxygen.
fields.mechanism: Yttrium has a high oxygen affinity and is known to segregate to surfaces and grain boundaries, forming a stable, slow-growing Y2O3 layer that acts as an effective barrier to oxygen ingress. This passivating oxide helps protect the underlying BCC matrix from oxidation without altering its bulk mechanical properties. The mechanism draws on principles from oxide dispersion strengthening and surface segregation phenomena observed in high-temperature alloys.
fields.predicted_outcome: Enhanced oxidation resistance at 1000 °C with a significantly reduced oxide scale growth (lower weight gain) while maintaining the alloy’s useful balance between ductility and yield strength. The protective effect is expected to mitigate oxidation-related degradation by at least an order of magnitude compared to the unmodified alloy, within experimental uncertainty.
fields.baseline: Untreated as-cast HfNbTaTiZr which exhibits poor oxidation resistance at high temperatures.
fields.boundary: The yttrium addition must be kept low (≤2 at%) to avoid destabilizing the single BCC phase or inducing unwanted intermetallics. The passivation effect is confined to surface layers so that bulk solution strengthening is preserved.
fields.uncertainty: While yttrium is widely used in oxide-dispersion-strengthened systems, its behavior in the specific high-entropy BCC matrix and its exact segregation kinetics remain to be fully established.

Measure surface oxide composition (using XRD/EDS) and weight gain. Subsequently, perform room-temperature tensile testing and high-temperature compression testing to assess mechanical performance.

falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the yttrium-modified alloy does not form a coherent Y2O3 scale or if oxidation weight gain and degradation in mechanical properties exceed the performance of the unmodified alloy by more than 15%, the hypothesis is falsified.

top3.label: C1
top3.builds_on: the finding from the paper that a fluorine-based surface treatment can promote a protective oxide scale—in the Ti-45Al-8.5Nb system—by modifying the surface chemistry to favor selective oxidation; here the concept is extended by using an alternative fluorinating agent (NH4HF2) that produces more stable oxyfluoride intermediates on a different alloy system.
top3.what_is_new: This hypothesis replaces NaF with NH4HF2 to leverage the formation of oxyfluoride species (rather than uncertain pure Hf- or Zr-fluorides), thereby addressing the critique regarding volatility differences and extending the fluorine-effect mechanism to a non-Al system by inducing a protective scale composed primarily of HfO2 and supplementary refractory oxides.

fields.hypothesis: A modified aqueous treatment using a dilute ammonium bifluoride (NH4HF2) solution can be applied to cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr to induce the formation of a thin, fluorine‐rich oxyfluoride precursor on the surface. Upon subsequent high-temperature oxidation, this precursor converts into a tight, adherent oxide scale comprised primarily of HfO2 augmented by stable Nb- and Ta-oxides.
fields.material_initial_state: Cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr with 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility and yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C, which in its untreated state develops a loose, porous oxide scale during high-temperature exposure.
fields.intervention: Spray the alloy surface with an aqueous NH4HF2 solution (~0.15 mol/L), then dry it prior to high-temperature oxidation.
fields.conditions: Subsequent isothermal oxidation in static air at 1000 °C for 100 hours; mechanical testing under the same strain rate and loading conditions as the cast state.
fields.structural_mediator: A fluorine‐rich oxyfluoride precursor surface layer that, when oxidized, converts into a dense mixed oxide scale (predominantly HfO2 with contributions from Nb- and Ta-derived oxides) known for its low oxygen diffusivity.
fields.mechanism: The NH4HF2 solution decomposes upon drying and interacts with surface Hf, Nb and Ta to form oxyfluoride species that are less volatile than pure metal fluorides. These species act as nucleation sites during oxidation, promoting the rapid formation of a coherent HfO2-based oxide. The presence of Nb/Ta oxides further enhances scale adhesion and limits oxygen ingress, while avoiding fluidity or excessive brittleness that could impair mechanical performance. This mechanism deliberately exploits the lower volatility of oxyfluorides compared to pure HfF, addressing the critique concerning uncertainty in Hf and Zr fluoride behavior (cf. PMC9030595::web::012).
fields.predicted_outcome: A measurable reduction in oxidation weight gain (targeting at least a 50% reduction relative to untreated samples) and the formation of an oxide scale that is adherent and capable of preserving the alloy’s mechanical properties.
fields.baseline: Untreated HfNbTaTiZr forms a porous, non-coherent oxide layer that permits deep oxygen penetration and degrades performance at high temperature.
fields.boundary: The intervention is designed for oxidation in air around 1000 °C for up to 100 hours. Excessively high concentrations of NH4HF2 or deviations in application may lead to over-etching or formation of too thick a modified layer, which might compromise ductility.
fields.uncertainty: While the formation of oxyfluoride precursors has precedence in systems requiring controlled fluorination, the precise kinetics of conversion on a multi-element refractory alloy remain moderately uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of cast HfNbTaTiZr specimens: treat one group by spraying with 0.15 mol/L NH4HF2 aqueous solution and leave the other untreated. Subject both groups to isothermal oxidation in air at 1000 °C for 100 hours. Post-oxidation, characterize the oxide scale by SEM/EDS and XRD, and measure weight gain and mechanical properties (tensile ductility and yield strength).

Phase composition and microstructure of the oxide scale (SEM/EDS, XRD)
Room-temperature tensile ductility and high-temperature yield strength
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the NH4HF2-treated specimens do not achieve at least a 50% reduction in oxidation weight gain, show a non-coherent or spalled oxide scale, or if there is a measurable degradation in mechanical properties relative to controls, the hypothesis is falsified.
